stem: Why is a PA chest exposure made at the end of deep inspiration?
options: To depress the diaphragm and show as much lung as possible
To show the ribs below the diaphragm
explanation: Deep inspiration moves the diaphragm down so the lungs are fully expanded and more ribs show above the diaphragm.

stem: Chest radiographs are taken with the patient erect mainly so that
options: the diaphragm moves to its lowest position and air-fluid levels are shown
explanation: Erect, the abdominal organs drop, letting the diaphragm descend, and any air or fluid settles into visible levels.

stem: A routine lateral chest is usually taken with which side against the image receptor?
options: Either side, it makes no difference
explanation: With the left side against the receptor, the heart is closer to it and less magnified.

stem: A small amount of free air in the abdomen is best shown with an AP projection in which position?
explanation: Lying on the left side, free air rises to the right side and is seen against the liver.

stem: A small amount of fluid in the pleural cavity is best shown in the lateral decubitus position with the
explanation: Fluid settles to the dependent side, so the affected side goes down; air rises, so for air the affected side goes up.

stem: A small pneumothorax is best shown in the lateral decubitus position with the
explanation: Air rises to the uppermost side, so the affected side is placed up.

stem: The scapular Y projection of the shoulder is used mainly to show
options: anterior or posterior dislocation of the humerus
explanation: The Y is formed by the acromion, coracoid and scapular body; a dislocated humeral head lies off its center, anterior or posterior.

stem: For the AP oblique projection (Grashey method) of the glenoid fossa, the patient is rotated
options: 15 degrees away from the affected side
30 degrees away from the affected side
explanation: Turning about 35 to 45 degrees toward the affected side opens the glenohumeral joint and shows the glenoid fossa in profile.

stem: The tunnel view (PA axial, Camp-Coventry method) of the knee demonstrates the
explanation: The tunnel view is used to demonstrate the intercondyloid fossa.

stem: For a lateral knee, the central ray is usually angled
explanation: About 5 degrees cephalad keeps the medial femoral condyle from obscuring the joint space.

stem: A 45-degree oblique of the lumbar spine is performed mainly to show the
explanation: The lumbar zygapophyseal (apophyseal) joints lie at an angle to the midsagittal plane and open in the 45-degree oblique.

stem: The lumbar intervertebral foramina are best demonstrated in which projection?
explanation: Lumbar intervertebral foramina lie at 90 degrees to the midsagittal plane, so they are parallel to the central ray in the lateral.

stem: The cervical intervertebral foramina are best demonstrated in
explanation: Cervical intervertebral foramina lie at about 45 degrees to the midsagittal plane, so they open in 45-degree obliques.

stem: The AP open-mouth projection demonstrates
options: the bodies of C3 to C7
the atlas and axis (C1 and C2)
explanation: With the mouth open, the teeth and skull are moved out of the way of C1, C2 and the odontoid process.

stem: In the parietoacanthial projection (Waters method), the orbitomeatal line forms what angle with the image receptor?
explanation: With the chin raised so the OML is 37 degrees to the IR, the petrous pyramids project below the maxillary sinuses.

stem: The PA projection (Caldwell method) is used to demonstrate the
options: maxillary sinuses free of the petrous ridges
explanation: The Caldwell PA shows the frontal sinuses and the anterior ethmoid sinuses.

stem: The AP axial projection (Towne method) of the skull, with the central ray 30 degrees caudad to the OML, best demonstrates the
explanation: The caudal angle projects the frontal and facial bones downward, so the occipital bone is seen without superimposition.

stem: Which skull projection demonstrates the cranial base, sphenoid sinuses, atlas and odontoid process?
explanation: In the submentovertical projection the central ray passes up through the base of the skull.

stem: Which maneuver better demonstrates the carpal scaphoid?
explanation: Ulnar flexion, often with the fist clenched, straightens the scaphoid and opens the spaces around it.

stem: The medial (internal) oblique projection of the elbow best demonstrates the
options: radial head free of the ulna
explanation: Internal rotation projects the coronoid process free of superimposition; the lateral (external) oblique frees the radial head.

stem: For a lateral projection of the humerus, the epicondyles are placed
explanation: Internal rotation puts the epicondyles perpendicular to the IR and superimposed, giving a true lateral.

stem: For an AP projection of the forearm, the hand is
explanation: Supination keeps the radius and ulna parallel; pronation would cross the radius over the ulna.

stem: For the mortise projection of the ankle, the leg and foot are rotated
explanation: Medial rotation of 15 to 20 degrees places the malleoli parallel to the IR and opens the whole mortise joint.

stem: The ankle mortise is formed by the
explanation: The ankle joint is formed by the tibia, the fibula and the talus; the calcaneus is not part of it.

stem: The subtalar joint is formed by the
explanation: The talocalcaneal (subtalar) joint is a three-faceted joint between the talus and the calcaneus.

stem: For the axial (plantodorsal) projection of the calcaneus, the central ray is directed
explanation: The central ray is angled 40 degrees cephalad to the long axis of the foot.

stem: For an AP hip, the affected leg is rotated internally 15 to 20 degrees to
options: show the lesser trochanter in profile
place the femoral neck parallel to the IR
explanation: Internal rotation brings the femoral neck parallel to the IR so its full length is shown without foreshortening.

stem: If a hip fracture is suspected, the lateral projection taken without moving the leg is the
options: AP pelvis with the legs abducted
explanation: The cross-table axiolateral is done without moving the injured leg; the frog-leg position requires moving it.

stem: During an upper GI series, which position shows a barium-filled pylorus and duodenum?
explanation: In the RAO position, barium drains toward the pylorus and duodenum.

stem: For an esophagram, which oblique position places the esophagus between the spine and the heart?
explanation: The RAO position projects the barium-filled esophagus between the vertebral column and the heart.

stem: During a barium enema, the LPO position best demonstrates the
explanation: The LPO (and its counterpart the RAO) opens the right colic flexure; the RPO and LAO open the left colic flexure.

stem: During IV urography, the prone position is recommended mainly to demonstrate
options: the upper poles of the kidneys
explanation: Prone, the ureters are dependent and fill better with contrast.

stem: In retrograde pyelography, the contrast agent is introduced
options: into the ureters through a cystoscope
explanation: A retrograde pyelogram fills the collecting system through ureteral catheters placed during cystoscopy; an IVU uses an intravenous injection.

stem: A patient lying on the back is in which position?
explanation: Supine means lying on the back; prone means lying face down.

stem: In the RAO position, which surface of the patient is against the image receptor?
explanation: Right anterior oblique: the right front of the body is closest to the receptor.

stem: For a PA chest, the shoulders are relaxed and depressed in order to
options: move the clavicles below the lung apices
explanation: Relaxed, depressed shoulders bring the clavicles down below the apices, so the tops of the lungs are not hidden.

stem: Ribs below the diaphragm are radiographed on
explanation: Expiration raises the diaphragm, showing the lower ribs against the abdomen; ribs above the diaphragm are taken on inspiration.

stem: To open the S-shaped sigmoid colon in an AP projection during a barium enema, the central ray is directed
explanation: A 30- to 40-degree cephalad angle elongates the sigmoid so its loops do not overlap; for a PA projection the angle is reversed.

stem: The sternum is radiographed in which position, so that it is projected over the heart shadow?
explanation: A slight RAO projects the sternum over the heart, whose uniform density makes it visible; in a PA it would be hidden by the spine.

stem: In an AP oblique (LPO) projection of the sacroiliac joints, which joint is demonstrated?
options: The right, the side farther from the IR
explanation: For the sacroiliac joints, the AP obliques show the joint farther from the IR: the LPO shows the right joint.

stem: To demonstrate acromioclavicular joint separation, AP projections of both joints are taken
options: with the central ray 45 degrees caudad
explanation: Weights hung from the wrists pull the shoulders down and show a separation that may not appear without them.

stem: When the open-mouth projection does not show the upper odontoid process well, which projection can supplement it?
options: AP or PA through the foramen magnum (Fuchs or Judd method)
explanation: The Fuchs (AP) and Judd (PA) methods project the odontoid within the foramen magnum.

stem: For a PA oblique projection of the hand, the fingers should be
options: parallel to the IR, to open the joints
explanation: Fingers kept parallel to the IR, often on a sponge, show the interphalangeal joints open without foreshortening.

stem: For an AP (dorsoplantar) projection of the foot, the central ray is directed
explanation: Angling the central ray 10 degrees posteriorly puts it perpendicular to the metatarsals and opens the tarsometatarsal joints.

stem: A tangential (sunrise) projection of the patella shows the
explanation: The tangential projection shows the patella in profile and the joint space between it and the femur.

stem: A lateral cervical spine is usually taken at what SID, to reduce magnification from the large OID?
explanation: The shoulder keeps the spine far from the IR, so a 72-in SID is used to reduce magnification.

stem: The routine lateral projection of the cervical spine is also known as the
explanation: The Grandy method is the routine lateral cervical spine. Fuchs and Judd show the odontoid; Ottonello is the moving-jaw AP.

stem: For the AP axial projection of the cervical spine, the central ray is directed
explanation: A 15- to 20-degree cephalad angle matches the slope of the vertebral bodies and opens the intervertebral disk spaces.

stem: Which of the following helps reduce breast exposure during scoliosis examinations?
explanation: Scoliosis patients are often young and imaged repeatedly. A fast imaging system, compensating filters and the PA projection all lower breast dose.

stem: Hysterosalpingography demonstrates
options: the uterus and the patency of the uterine tubes
explanation: Contrast introduced into the uterus outlines its cavity and shows whether the uterine (fallopian) tubes are open.
